title: Dominic and the Portrait
premise: Silas Oyelaran, a late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week—each one asking her to read back something they once said on air. When her childhood imaginary friend Dominic appears on her porch, unchanged after thirty years, she realizes he is not a memory but a collector: every secret she has ever kept from her listeners' deaths was an invitation, and tonight the frost is writing his contract onto her windows. To survive until sunrise she must broadcast the truth of what she invited in—the hit-and-run she witnessed as a child and buried—and let justice, not silence, be the price of survival.
about_author: Noor Eriksen is a former overnight radio producer from coastal Maine who swears half her show's callers sounded like they were calling from somewhere colder than the grave. She writes horror about small towns, old debts, and the things that wait politely at the edge of porch lights.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. During her 2 a.m. call-in show, a familiar voice requests a song—belonging to Marla Voss, who died six days ago. Silas checks the obituary live on air and her hands shake through the weather report. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: The Log
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She begins documenting every anomalous call in a notebook, treating documentation as prayer. Three more dead listeners call; each asks her to repeat words they said on air years ago. Emotional beat: obsessive comfort curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Coming home before dawn, she finds a small figure waiting on her steps—a boy in a yellow raincoat, exactly as she drew him at age seven. He says only, 'You kept my seat.' Emotional beat: vertigo between tenderness and terror.

chapters.title: Dominic
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, with flashback threads. She remembers inventing Dominic after the accident she never told anyone about. Now he sits in her kitchen drinking nothing, watching her write. Emotional beat: the intimacy of being known by something wrong.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Silas and a dead caller, Ruth. Ruth explains the rules gently: the dead can only ask for what was spoken aloud. What was never said belongs to someone else entirely. Emotional beat: dawning understanding that silence has a creditor.

chapters.title: The Frost Pattern
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Frost blooms across her windows in shapes she recognizes from childhood drawings—her drawings. Each pane shows a scene she's never confessed. The last pane is blank, waiting. Emotional beat: claustrophobic inevitability.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, first time. He recounts the night in 1994 when seven-year-old Silas whispered to him alone: the car, the man inside, the body on Fenwick Road. He did not create himself; she invited him with a secret. Emotional beat: chilling revelation that imagination was a door.

chapters.title: The Man on Fenwick Road
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Silas's POV. The full accident: Councilman Aldous Wren, drunk, striking a pedestrian; Silas hiding in the hedge; Wren finding her and buying her silence with a look, then decades of quiet favors. Emotional beat: the corruption of power shown as a slow purchase.

chapters.title: Favors
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She researches her own life and finds Wren's fingerprints everywhere: her scholarship, her station license, her landlord. Her whole visible life was hush money. Emotional beat: grief for a self built on someone else's crime.

chapters.title: The Dead Want Airtime
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The dead callers grow insistent—they don't want songs anymore; they want the truth read on air. The station manager threatens to fire her for the 'prank calls.' Emotional beat: pressure mounting from both worlds.

chapters.title: Wren Calls In
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Aldous Wren, now dying of cancer, phones the show under a fake name and asks her to read a statement denying everything. She recognizes his voice instantly. Emotional beat: cold fury meeting calculated charm.

chapters.title: Seat Kept Warm
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic explains the deadline: sunrise ends the invitation window. If she confesses publicly, the debt transfers to Wren. If she stays silent, the frost finishes its pattern and takes her instead. Emotional beat: terrible clarity of the bargain.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Station engineer Dev's POV. Dev notices the transmitter drawing impossible power at night and dead air behaving like a held breath. He warns Silas something is living in the signal. Emotional beat: outside confirmation that this is real.

chapters.title: The Blank Pane
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The final frost pane begins filling in—with her face, aged, mouth open mid-broadcast. Dominic stands behind her reflection, patient. She has one night left. Emotional beat: mortality made decorative.

chapters.title: Confession Drafts
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She writes and burns four drafts of her confession, each time flinching from naming Wren. Dominic reads the ashes like tea leaves and says, 'Almost.' Emotional beat: the difficulty of truth even when survival demands it.

chapters.title: Wren's Visit
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Silas and Wren. Wren arrives at the station with lawyers and a settlement check, offering her own show in any market she wants. He knows about the calls. He knows about Dominic. He's been paying longer than she knew. Emotional beat: power's final, rotting offer.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She locks herself in the studio at midnight, frost climbing the glass, dead callers holding the phone lines open like a choir. She begins reading the log aloud—all of it, names, dates, the road, the car. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into testimony.

chapters.title: The Name
chapters.summary: Climax, Silas's POV. Live on air, she says 'Aldous Wren killed a man on Fenwick Road, and I watched, and I was bought.' The frost shatters outward. Dominic turns toward the sound of the name like a compass needle. Emotional beat: liberation and horror in one breath.

chapters.title: Collection
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The debt transfers. Dominic leaves through the studio door—not toward Silas, but toward the hospital across town where Wren's machines are failing. The dead callers sign off one by one, grateful. Emotional beat: justice arriving without mercy or ceremony.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Dawn finds her alive in a wrecked studio, fired by noon, famous by evening. The notebook survives; the recordings do not—only people heard them. Emotional beat: exhausted, costly relief.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, weeks later. Wren dies; the investigation reopens; some believe her, many don't. She loses the career built on hush money and starts a podcast called The Log, reading listener confessions no court will hear. Emotional beat: justice outside the law as ongoing work, not victory.

chapters.title: The Empty Seat
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Silas's POV. On the first frost of next winter, she sets two cups of cocoa on the porch—one for her, one for a seat no one fills. The panes stay clear. But the radio, off, hums once, softly, like someone clearing their throat. Emotional beat: peace with an open door.
